headline: Hot Mix 5 co-founder Kenny 'Jammin' Jason has died
caption:
Kenny 'Jammin' Jason, a founding member of the Hot Mix 5, has died. "I miss you already."

Farley 'Jackmaster' Funk announced his death on 19 November. No cause was disclosed. Jason released the six-track instrumental EP 'Jam Tracks' in 1985 and co-founded Hot Mix 5 Records in 1986, and DJ Kenny Jammin Jason Boulevard was named in his honour.

Which Hot Mix 5-era Chicago record still gets played in your sets? 👇

article.headline: Hot Mix 5 co-founder Kenny 'Jammin' Jason has died
article.standfirst: Kenny 'Jammin' Jason has died. The Chicago DJ, producer and remixer was a founding member of the Hot Mix 5. Fellow member Farley 'Jackmaster' Funk announced the news on November 19. No cause of death was disclosed.
body: Kenny 'Jammin' Jason has died. The Chicago DJ, producer and remixer was a founding member of the Hot Mix 5, the collective whose radio broadcasts introduced wider audiences to house music. Fellow member Farley 'Jackmaster' Funk announced the news on November 19, 2026. No cause of death has been disclosed.

In a Facebook tribute, Farley 'Jackmaster' Funk called Jason his greatest musical mentor and said he thought of him as a brother. "I miss you already," he wrote. "RIP. This really hits harder than anyone could know, and I'll tell this story if I'm alive to tell it."

Jason built his reputation on local radio and at mobile disco parties before joining WBMX-FM's Hot Mix 5. The collective was founded in 1981, and its members were Jason, Farley 'Jackmaster' Funk, Mickey 'Mixin' Oliver, Ralphi Rosario and Scott 'Smokin' Silz. Their broadcasts brought house music, and the mixing techniques coming out of Chicago's clubs, to a wider audience while the city's early house scene was still forming.

He also worked in the studio. In 1985 he released 'Jam Tracks', a six-track instrumental EP. His production credits include work with Liz Torres, and he made 'Can U Dance' with Fast Eddie. In 1986 he co-founded Hot Mix 5 Records with Oliver and Rosario, which gave music from Chicago's developing house scene another outlet.

Jason kept DJing in the decades that followed and stayed connected to Chicago radio and the local music community. His contribution was recognised with the naming of DJ Kenny Jammin Jason Boulevard, and in 2016 he reunited with his Hot Mix 5 colleagues for the collective's 35th-anniversary celebration.

points.title: The Hot Mix 5 line-up
points.text: Founded in 1981, the WBMX-FM collective was Jason, Farley 'Jackmaster' Funk, Mickey 'Mixin' Oliver, Ralphi Rosario and Scott 'Smokin' Silz. Their broadcasts introduced wider audiences to house and the mixing techniques coming out of Chicago's clubs.

points.title: In the studio
points.text: In 1985 Jason released 'Jam Tracks', a six-track instrumental EP. His production credits include work with Liz Torres, and he collaborated with Fast Eddie on 'Can U Dance'.

points.title: His legacy
points.text: In 1986 he co-founded Hot Mix 5 Records with Oliver and Rosario. DJ Kenny Jammin Jason Boulevard was named in his honour, and in 2016 he reunited with the crew for its 35th anniversary.

article.headline: Indira Paganotto remixes Depeche Mode for vinyl box set
article.standfirst: Depeche Mode's singles from 'Memento Mori' have been remixed by a group of electronic artists that includes Indira Paganotto, Daniel Avery and Boris Brejcha.
body: The singles from Depeche Mode's album 'Memento Mori' have been remixed by a group of electronic artists, with Indira Paganotto, Daniel Avery and Boris Brejcha among the names involved.
The new versions are coming out as part of a special 12" vinyl box set that gathers the remixed singles in one physical package.

Paganotto, Avery and Brejcha are not the only contributors. More artists have also remixed tracks for the project, which means the collection reaches well beyond a single remix or a one-off reworking.

For DJs who still play records, the format matters: a 12" box set puts these versions straight onto vinyl, the medium club selectors have relied on for decades, instead of leaving them as streaming-only releases.
It also puts three very different names from today's electronic scene side by side on one Depeche Mode release, all working from the same source material: the 'Memento Mori' singles.
HARDMAG will follow the release as more of it comes out, including the full list of remixers on the box set.

headline: 'You don't belong here': how Rane met the Steelworkerz
caption:
A bouncer behind a steel door in a Manhattan alley told Rane's engineers they didn't belong.

When they said the Steelworkerz had invited them, his expression changed and they were let in. Inside, Rick Jeffs got his first look at true performance scratch mixing: DJs using turntables as musical instruments. The mixers those DJs had back then often lacked the features they wanted and struggled to hold up in competition, and that was the gap Rane set out to fill.

Magnetic or old-school contact crossfader: what difference do you actually feel when you cut? 👇

Source: @attackmag
📸 via @attackmag

#rane #turntablism #scratchdj #djmixer #djgear #djhistory

article.headline: 'You don't belong here': how Rane met the Steelworkerz
article.standfirst: As Rane turns 45, Principal Design Engineer Rick Jeffs told Attack Magazine where its scratch mixers began. Its first DJ mixer, the 1986 MP 24, was built at the request of Richard Long, Studio 54's sound designer.
body: A taxi dropped Rane's engineers in a dark alley in front of a large steel door. A bouncer looked them over and said: "You don't belong here." They told him the Steelworkerz had invited them to talk about a new mixer, and he let them in. As Rane turns 45, Principal Design Engineer Rick Jeffs told Attack Magazine that this trip started the company's move into turntablism.

Rane was founded in 1981. Its first DJ mixer, the MP 24, came out in 1986 at the request of Richard Long, the sound designer for Studio 54 and many other clubs. Jeffs describes it as a purely analog design built from op-amps, resistors and capacitors.

The Steelworkerz, a crew made up of Brian Lane (Big Wiz), Doug Coen (Sugarcuts), Marz1 and Peter Parker, asked Rane to build the ultimate scratch mixer. The first meeting took place at Tableturns, an open-format competition in lower Manhattan. Jeffs says it was his first real look at performance scratch mixing, with DJs using turntables as musical instruments. The next night the two sides sketched ideas for a battle mixer in a South Bronx apartment.

According to Jeffs, the mixers available at the time often lacked the features turntablists wanted and often had durability problems under competition-style use. Rane's answer was the TTM 54. The TTM 56 came next, with the industry's first non-contact magnetic crossfader and improved full-cut channel faders. Jeffs chose magnetic sensing over resistive, inductive and optical designs because it was robust, simple and largely immune to environmental contamination. Rane later refined it for better linearity and resolution.

Later Rane mixers added dual USB, which lets two DJs hand over between laptops without stopping the music. That feature has also spread across the industry. Jeffs says the computer connection, through platforms such as Serato and Engine, may be the biggest change since the analog MP 24.

points.title: Why magnetic won
points.text: Jeffs weighed resistive, inductive, optical and magnetic sensing. Resistive faders wear, get noisy and develop dead spots. Optical adds complexity. Magnetic was robust, simple and largely immune to the contamination that often affected conventional faders.

points.title: From op-amps to DSP
points.text: The MP 24 was purely analog: op-amps, resistors and capacitors, with no firmware or drivers. Modern mixers digitize audio at the input, process it digitally and convert it back at the outputs, with MCUs monitoring the controls.

points.title: Two laptops, no gap
points.text: Later Rane mixers added dual USB, so two DJs can stay connected and hand over between laptops without stopping the music. Like the magnetic crossfader, it became widely adopted across the industry.

posted.title: “You Don’t Belong Here”: How Rane Got Into Turntablism
posted.headline: 'You don't belong here': how Rane met the Steelworkerz

headline: Innerbloom leaves the dancefloor in Hans Zimmer's hands
caption:
Eleven years on, 'Innerbloom' trades the synths for timpani, until the motif comes back.

Every earlier version of RÜFÜS DU SOL's signature track stayed in dance music. 'Innerbloom XI' leaves it: Hans Zimmer and Bleeding Fingers rebuilt it as a nine-minute orchestral piece, and it is the only official release for the anniversary. The video is by Katzki and Thomás Blanchard, based on Jack Vanzet's Bloom artwork, which he updated for the release.

Do orchestral reworks of dance classics add something, or should these tracks stay on the dancefloor? 👇

article.headline: Innerbloom leaves the dancefloor in Hans Zimmer's hands
article.standfirst: Previous versions of 'Innerbloom' stayed in dance music. Hans Zimmer and his collective Bleeding Fingers move it into an orchestral format: 'Innerbloom XI', the only official release for its 11th anniversary.
body: Every previous version of RÜFÜS DU SOL's 'Innerbloom' stayed inside dance music. The new one doesn't. 'Innerbloom XI', made with composer Hans Zimmer and his collective Bleeding Fingers, moves the track into an orchestral format. It is the only official release marking the song's 11th anniversary, and it is out now on streaming platforms.

The arrangement runs nine minutes. Tyrone Lindqvist's original vocals stay at its centre, set against horns, woodwinds, strings and timpani, with a xylophone break along the way. Near the close, the original synth motif comes back, the moment that ties the orchestral version to the one people know from the dancefloor.
The release comes with a music video by visual artists Katzki and Thomás Blanchard. It is inspired by Jack Vanzet's original Bloom cover art, which Vanzet updated for the occasion.

'Innerbloom' first came out more than a decade ago and has since passed 1.2 billion streams worldwide. The anniversary version follows a global tour on which RÜFÜS DU SOL sold out multiple nights at Madison Square Garden in New York and the Kia Forum in Los Angeles, a sign of the scale the band now works at.

For a track this tied to club and festival moments, the decision to mark the anniversary with a single orchestral rework, and nothing else, is the point of the release: the anniversary goes to a rework that leaves dance music altogether.

posted.title: Hans Zimmer reworks RÜFÜS DU SOL’s ‘Innerbloom’ for track’s 11th anniversary

headline: Years of shared gigs, one record: Capriati, Troxler, TB-203
caption:
After years of sharing booths, Joseph Capriati and @stroxler have made their first studio record together.

‘The Afterlife’ brings in TB-203, who is linked to Troxler through Slacker 85, and is out now on Metamorfosi Records. The original pairs a prominent bassline with acid-driven rhythms for late-night clubs. The Deeper Mix starts restrained and percussive, then gets heavier.

article.headline: Years of shared gigs, one record: Capriati, Troxler, TB-203
article.standfirst: Joseph Capriati and Seth Troxler have made their first studio collaboration, ‘The Afterlife’, out now on Metamorfosi Records. It follows years of shared performances, including at Capriati's Metamorfosi Ibiza residency. TB-203 (Tommy Bones) joins, linked to Troxler through Slacker 85, which released his self-titled debut album.
body: Joseph Capriati and Seth Troxler have released their first studio collaboration. ‘The Afterlife’ is a two-track release made with TB-203, the alias of Tommy Bones, and it is out now on Metamorfosi Records.
The record follows years of the two playing together. Their friendship and musical relationship grew through shared performances, including appearances at Capriati's Metamorfosi Ibiza residency.
TB-203's connection with Troxler runs through the Slacker 85 catalog, which includes Tommy Bones' self-titled debut album under the TB-203 name.

‘The Afterlife’ was produced across studios in Tulum, London and Naples, and connects influences from Naples, Detroit and New York. The original mix centres on a prominent bassline, with atmospheric vocals and acid-driven rhythms, and develops a darker, hypnotic sound suited to late-night club settings.
The second track, ‘The Afterlife (Deeper Mix)’, opens with a more restrained, percussive take before developing into a heavier arrangement, with driving rhythms and an arpeggiated bassline.

posted.title: Joseph Capriati, Seth Troxler, and TB-203 unite on ‘The Afterlife’
